# Remote trust

Six things a remote link keeps apart (v0.4.1 §51.3). Each says what a reader may conclude when it is in place and — the column that does the work — what a reader may not. §7.3 is why: the transport identity and the runtime identity are different fields, one is a cryptographic credential and the other is a self-report, and §65.1 and §65.2 are the two ways confusing them goes wrong. Rendered from `docs/spec/hardening/remote_trust.yaml`, which the documentation gate reads as well.

| Concept | Establishes | Does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| **SSH-carried stdio transport** | OpenSSH authenticated the far host, against your own `known_hosts`, before Ono saw a single byte. The channel is `ono --agent` on the far side reading a pipe OpenSSH already trusts, so the network peer is authenticated by something outside Ono and Ono says so rather than claiming it. | Ono never sees the key OpenSSH accepted, so this link has no `transport_fingerprint` and `authenticated` is false on it. §4.3 requires the trust source to be described accurately — "peer key visible to ono: no" — and forbids borrowing OpenSSH's verification as Ono's own. There is no client authorization on this path either: the far side's policy is the SSH account's. |
| **Direct mutual-TLS transport** | Both ends proved possession of a persistent key over TLS 1.3, before Ono's own `Hello` (§13.1). This is the only transport where Ono itself did the authenticating, and it is the only one where `authenticated` is true and `transport_fingerprint` names a key. | Encryption is not authentication and authentication is not permission. §65.1 names "TLS means authenticated" a failure mode, and §9.1 names the other half: holding a private key proves who you are, never that the operator wants you here. A mutually authenticated client is still refused until it is authorized. There is no flag that turns client authentication off (§7.4). |
| **Server host pinning** | The key the far side proved it holds matches a trust decision somebody recorded for that host. A different machine answering for the same name is refused with `remote.host_key_changed`, because a changed key is indistinguishable from an interception. | A pin is about the *server*. It says nothing about whether this client may connect, which is the server's own decision, and nothing about what this client may then do. Re-trusting after a real key change is a separate deliberate command rather than a prompt (§2.9). |
| **Client authorization** | The operator of the agent host recorded that this authenticated fingerprint may connect, and what it may do: observation by default (§9.4), and exactly the action capability ids that were granted by name (§9.5). This is the only thing on the list that grants authority. | It is not authentication and does not replace it — §2.2 puts authentication first, and an unauthenticated peer has no identity to authorize. It is also not the capability negotiation: §10.2 refuses at dispatch as well, so a client that constructs a request the offer omitted gains nothing (§65.3). |
| **Runtime user and UID metadata** | What the far side says it is running as: `runtime_user`, `runtime_uid`, `runtime_elevated`. Useful context when reading results — a value observed as root is a different observation from one observed as a service account. | It grants nothing. §7.3 keeps it in separate fields from the transport identity for this reason, and §2.1 forbids a self-report from satisfying the word authenticated: the far side is the one telling you, and §65.2 names authorization decided by a client's self-reported identity a forbidden failure mode. |
| **Capability negotiation** | Which targets and capabilities the far side offered this connection. The offer is already filtered by the client's authorization (§10.1), so an unauthorized client is not told what it is missing. | The offer is a view of the policy, never the policy itself. §10.2 requires the same check at dispatch, and §65.3 names negotiation-only authorization a forbidden failure mode. A target appearing in an offer is also not a promise the provider will answer: a denied door renders as a locked door. |

## SSH-carried stdio transport

OpenSSH authenticated the far host, against your own `known_hosts`, before Ono saw a single byte. The channel is `ono --agent` on the far side reading a pipe OpenSSH already trusts, so the network peer is authenticated by something outside Ono and Ono says so rather than claiming it.

**It does not establish.** Ono never sees the key OpenSSH accepted, so this link has no `transport_fingerprint` and `authenticated` is false on it. §4.3 requires the trust source to be described accurately — "peer key visible to ono: no" — and forbids borrowing OpenSSH's verification as Ono's own. There is no client authorization on this path either: the far side's policy is the SSH account's.

Operated by `link host`.

Boundary: `remote.ssh.transport`. Fixed by v0.4.1 §4.3, §51.3.

## Direct mutual-TLS transport

Both ends proved possession of a persistent key over TLS 1.3, before Ono's own `Hello` (§13.1). This is the only transport where Ono itself did the authenticating, and it is the only one where `authenticated` is true and `transport_fingerprint` names a key.

**It does not establish.** Encryption is not authentication and authentication is not permission. §65.1 names "TLS means authenticated" a failure mode, and §9.1 names the other half: holding a private key proves who you are, never that the operator wants you here. A mutually authenticated client is still refused until it is authorized. There is no flag that turns client authentication off (§7.4).

Operated by `link host`.

Boundary: `remote.tcp.transport`. Fixed by v0.4.1 §7.1, §13.1, §13.3, §51.3.

## Server host pinning

The key the far side proved it holds matches a trust decision somebody recorded for that host. A different machine answering for the same name is refused with `remote.host_key_changed`, because a changed key is indistinguishable from an interception.

**It does not establish.** A pin is about the *server*. It says nothing about whether this client may connect, which is the server's own decision, and nothing about what this client may then do. Re-trusting after a real key change is a separate deliberate command rather than a prompt (§2.9).

Operated by `add host-key`, `get host-key`, `set host-key`, `remove host-key`.

Boundary: `remote.tcp.transport`. Fixed by v0.4.1 §51.3; spec §21.5.

## Client authorization

The operator of the agent host recorded that this authenticated fingerprint may connect, and what it may do: observation by default (§9.4), and exactly the action capability ids that were granted by name (§9.5). This is the only thing on the list that grants authority.

**It does not establish.** It is not authentication and does not replace it — §2.2 puts authentication first, and an unauthenticated peer has no identity to authorize. It is also not the capability negotiation: §10.2 refuses at dispatch as well, so a client that constructs a request the offer omitted gains nothing (§65.3).

Operated by `add client-key`, `get client-key`, `set client-key`, `remove client-key`.

Boundary: `remote.tcp.authorization`. Fixed by v0.4.1 §9, §10, §51.3.

## Runtime user and UID metadata

What the far side says it is running as: `runtime_user`, `runtime_uid`, `runtime_elevated`. Useful context when reading results — a value observed as root is a different observation from one observed as a service account.

**It does not establish.** It grants nothing. §7.3 keeps it in separate fields from the transport identity for this reason, and §2.1 forbids a self-report from satisfying the word authenticated: the far side is the one telling you, and §65.2 names authorization decided by a client's self-reported identity a forbidden failure mode.

Operated by `get link`.

Boundary: none — this is metadata, not a boundary. Fixed by v0.4.1 §7.3, §51.3.

## Capability negotiation

Which targets and capabilities the far side offered this connection. The offer is already filtered by the client's authorization (§10.1), so an unauthorized client is not told what it is missing.

**It does not establish.** The offer is a view of the policy, never the policy itself. §10.2 requires the same check at dispatch, and §65.3 names negotiation-only authorization a forbidden failure mode. A target appearing in an offer is also not a promise the provider will answer: a denied door renders as a locked door.

Operated by `link host`, `get link`.

Boundary: `provider.query`. Fixed by v0.4.1 §10.1, §10.2, §51.3.
